title: Contextual and Seasonal LSTMs for Time Series Anomaly Detection
one_liner: Spot hidden anomalies in single-value time series by splitting the signal into expected normal patterns plus suspicious noise.
lead: You monitor a server: every second it reports temperature or traffic volume—one number. When that number jumps unexpectedly, something broke. But a small spike at the wrong time is easy to miss. This paper teaches a model to learn what normal looks like (repeating seasonal patterns plus short-term trends) and flag whatever does not fit, catching both tiny spikes and slow creeping rises that old methods miss.

problem.h2: One number per second, two kinds of invisible anomalies
paras: A univariate time series is a sequence of single numbers arriving over time—temperature of a server, memory usage, request count. When something breaks, the number changes in a way that should stand out. But two kinds of anomalies hide: a small spike that lasts one or two seconds (gets buried in random noise), or a slow creep (rises 1% per hour, barely visible among the seasonal ups and downs of business hours). Older methods predict the next number and flag when reality misses the prediction—but on single numbers, there is barely enough information in any one moment to make a strong prediction.

A beginner might try: Just learn to predict the next value, and flag big gaps. This fails because the model has almost nothing to work with. Single numbers have no depth, no channels, no different features to cross-reference. If the model has seen only the past three numbers, it might see a pattern like (100, 105, 110) and guess 115—but if the season is 'morning peak traffic,' the real pattern repeats daily, not every second. The model misses the slow seasonal rhythm and gets fooled by random jitter or the creep of time.

callout.html: Single-value time series lack enough detail per timestamp, so models cannot tell seasonal patterns from anomalies.

steps.text: Strip out anomalies from the raw signal so seasonal patterns emerge clearly.
A neural memory reads repeating patterns (morning is high, night is low).
A second neural memory reads short-term drifts (is it trending up today?).
Combine seasonal estimate plus local trend to forecast what normal should be.
If actual value is far from normal, raise an alert.

object.h2: What the paper changes: the loss function
paras: The paper changes how the model learns. Instead of treating anomalies like random noise (and learning them anyway), the model first estimates and removes them, then learns only from clean normal data. This resets the training goal: fit a probabilistic (the model outputs uncertainty too, not just a guess) prediction of the true normal value, learned only from the scrubbed data.

hidden.h2: The noise signal: what does not belong
hidden.name: Decomposed anomaly noise
paras: The hidden quantity the paper tracks is the noise component that gets peeled away. Real time series contain seasonal patterns (repeating cycles), local trends (gradual changes), and anomalies (sudden breaks). The paper estimates which part of each value is 'anomalous noise' and which part is legitimate trend. This decomposition is not given by labels; the model infers it because the actual observations include anomalies but the seasonal and local branches' predictions should only reflect normal values.

During training, the paper uses anomaly masks (guesses about which timestamps are broken) to separate the signal. The loss function then computes prediction error only on timestamps the model thinks are normal, creating a feedback loop: if the noise estimate is right, fitting to the 'clean' subset trains both branches strongly on true patterns. The noise estimate is implicitly optimized to maximize this fit.

heat.caption: Darker cells show estimated anomaly noise; brighter cells show normal pattern.

reads.html: Think of a scratched record. Most seconds play the real song (seasonal + local trend), but some seconds are scratches (anomalies). The model learns to recognize the song well enough that it can guess when a sound is not the song, and ignore scratches during learning.

The noise decomposition strategy estimates a residual (the leftover after subtracting seasonal and local predictions) and uses anomaly masks (derived from this residual) to weight the loss function, so anomalous timestamps contribute less to how the model updates its numbers.

mechanism.h2: Why splitting into seasonal and local lets you catch hidden anomalies
paras: Here is the chain of cause-and-effect. On univariate data, a single predicted value carries very little information; the model cannot be confident. But if the model separates its task into two experts, each with a different memory of the past, each can find a different pattern. The seasonal branch reads the full history and asks, 'What time of day is it? What month? What is the typical value for this phase of the cycle?' It returns an estimate (e.g., 103 degrees for 2 PM). The local branch reads the recent short-term trend and asks, 'Are we warming or cooling right now? How fast?' It returns a delta (e.g., plus 2 degrees). Together, they predict 105 degrees (the sum of 103 and 2) in normal conditions.

The clever part: during training, the model also produces a guess for which timestamps are likely anomalies (by looking at how badly the two-branch prediction misses). It then retrains using only the 'normal' subset, refining both branch predictions on purely normal data. This breaks the anomaly's grip: a false alarm at 3 PM teaches the local branch to expect a warm afternoon, and the model learns the real seasonal rhythm instead of overfitting to the anomaly. Small spikes get ignored (they do not match any seasonal pattern and do not align with local trends, so they are marked noise), and slow creeps get caught (the local branch notices the daily trend is inching upward, and when a day hits its seasonal norm but the local branch says 'cooler than yesterday,' the combined prediction still does not match a true creep).
By cleaning the training signal, both branches learn the truth. When a new anomaly arrives (a value that hits neither seasonal pattern nor local trend), the prediction gap is large and obvious.

stages.s: Raw time series with anomalies mixed in
Estimate anomaly noise (which timestamps are broken)
Filter to clean subset, train seasonal branch on normal values
Filter to clean subset, train local branch on normal values
Combine predictions and refine noise estimate
Model that flags gaps between expected normal and actual value

math.words: total loss = weighted seasonal prediction error + weighted local prediction error, where weights zero out anomalous timestamps
math.equation: L = E[ w_i * (yhat_seasonal_i + yhat_local_i - y_i)^2 ], where w_i = 0 if timestamp i is anomalous, 1 if normal
symbols: seasonal branch prediction for timestamp i
local branch prediction (delta) for timestamp i
weight: 0 if anomaly detected, 1 if normal

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Timestamp 1 (normal): actual=103, seasonal=100, local=2, combined_pred=102, error=(102-103)^2=1.0, weight=1.0, loss contribution=1.0
Timestamp 2 (spike): actual=150, seasonal=100, local=2, combined_pred=102, error=(102-150)^2=2304, weight=0 (anomalous), loss contribution=0
Timestamp 3 (normal): actual=104, seasonal=100, local=3, combined_pred=103, error=(103-104)^2=1.0, weight=1.0, loss contribution=1.0
Total loss = 1.0 + 0 + 1.0 = 2.0. The spike is ignored; only normal timestamps guide learning.

math.note: The weight mask is the key: by zeroing the loss for flagged anomalies, the model learns clean patterns and simultaneously refines which timestamps are truly anomalous.

charts.title: Old method (predict + flag large gaps)
charts.note: Struggles because single-value prediction is weak and seasonal rhythm is invisible.

charts.title: This paper (decomposed two-branch prediction)
charts.note: Seasonal and local branches separately encode rhythm and trend, so both anomaly types become visible.

items.b: Seasonal branch fails if the pattern does not actually repeat.
items.html: If the data has no day-long or year-long rhythm (truly random walks), the seasonal branch learns nothing and both branches collapse to the same guess. The decomposition assumes a repeating cycle exists.

If the model guesses wrong about which timestamps are anomalies (e.g., it marks a true slow creep as 'normal' early on), both branches learn the creep as trend and the model never flags it. The feedback loop can entrench errors.

items.b: Local branch captures anomalies, not trends.
items.html: On short lookback windows, the local branch can overfit to recent anomalies if the noise mask is imperfect. If it learns 'yesterday spiked to 150, so today should be 140,' it has learned the anomaly's shadow, not the true local trend.

For best results, initialize the seasonal branch with known cycle lengths (hourly/daily/weekly), and tune the threshold for marking anomalies on a validation set from the same system. This anchors the decomposition in reality.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a univariate time series generator that produces (1) a strong seasonal cycle (e.g., daily warmth cycle: 20 degrees at midnight, 30 at noon, back to 20 at midnight), (2) a short-term trend (e.g., each day is 0.2 degrees warmer than the last), and (3) injected anomalies (random spikes or slow creeps at known times). Train a two-branch model (one reading full history, one reading recent history) to jointly minimize prediction error on 'normal' timestamps (given by a noisy mask). Record which anomaly timestamps the model flags. Compare against a single-branch baseline that has the same total model capacity but no semantic split.
demo.metric_eq: Detection rate = (anomalies correctly flagged) / (total injected anomalies); False alarm rate = (normal points wrongly flagged) / (total normal points); Goal: detection rate > 80%, false alarm rate < 5%
demo.closing: The demo must make it impossible to miss: the two-branch model's prediction on clean data hugs the true seasonal + trend signal, while the single-branch baseline's prediction is a blur, because it tries to fit to anomalies and true patterns at once.
